title: Permissions, chmod, umask & ownership
about: Reading and changing permission bits on files and directories, octal and symbolic modes, the umask, chown and chgrp, and the special bits.

questions.title: Three classes of users
questions.text: Every file has permissions for three classes of users. Which are they?

options.t: The owner (user), the owner's group, and everyone else (others).
options.why: The kernel checks them in that order and uses the first class that matches you.
Unix permissions are not organised by such roles.

options.t: Read users, write users and execute users.
options.why: Read/write/execute are the *permissions*, not the classes of people.

options.t: The creator, the last editor and the last reader.
options.why: Nothing like that is recorded.

questions.title: Reading a mode string
questions.text: Match each mode string of `ls -l` with what it tells you.

pairs.r: A regular file: owner rwx, group r-x, others r--
pairs.why: The first character is the file type, then three triplets.

pairs.r: A directory only its owner can use
pairs.why: Group and others have no permissions at all.
The `l` type; the permissions shown are not used.

pairs.r: A regular file readable only by its owner
pairs.why: Even the owner cannot write to it.

questions.title: Who is checked
questions.text: Your user owns a file with mode `---rw-rw-` (owner has nothing, group and others can read and write), and you are a member of its group. Can you read it?

options.t: No: you are the owner, so only the owner's (empty) permissions are checked, even though the others would allow it.
options.why: The kernel picks the first matching class, it does not add them up.

options.t: Yes, because the group permissions allow it.
options.why: The owner class wins, and it denies.

options.t: Yes, because the `others` class allows it.
options.why: Others apply only if you are neither owner nor group member.

options.t: Yes, because you can always read your own files.
options.why: Owning a file does not override its mode (only root ignores it).

questions.title: Root and permissions
questions.text: How do permission bits affect the user `root`?

options.t: Root can read and write anything, and can execute a file only if at least one execute bit is set.
options.why: Execute still needs an `x` somewhere.

options.t: Root is bound by the same checks as everyone else.
options.why: Root bypasses read and write checks.

options.t: Root can never read files with mode 000.
options.why: It can.

options.t: Root may execute any file whatever its mode.
options.why: A file with no `x` anywhere cannot be executed, even by root.

questions.text: What do the three permissions allow on an ordinary file?

options.t: `r` read the contents, `w` change the contents, `x` run it as a program.
options.why: For a script, reading is also needed when run via an interpreter.
Renaming and deleting depend on the directory, not on the file's bits.

items.why: `x` means "traverse" or "search".

questions.title: The three operators
questions.text: What is the difference between `chmod g+w f`, `chmod g-w f` and `chmod g=w f`?

options.t: Add write for the group, remove write from the group, set the group to exactly write and nothing else.
options.why: `=` replaces the whole triplet.

options.t: They all give the group write permission.
options.why: Only the first does so additively.
That is what `+` and `-` do.

options.t: `+` changes the owner, `-` changes the group.
options.why: The class letter chooses who, not the operator.

questions.title: chmod a-wx
questions.text: What does `chmod a-wx file` do?

options.t: Removes write and execute from the owner, the group and others.
options.why: `a` means all three classes.
Read is not touched.

options.t: Sets exactly write and execute for everybody.
options.why: That would be `a=wx`.

options.t: Adds write and execute for everybody.
options.why: The minus removes.

questions.title: Combined changes
questions.text: What is the result of `chmod u-x,go+w n` on a file with mode `rwxr-----`?

options.why: The owner loses `x`; group and others gain `w`.
The owner's `x` was removed.
The `go+w` part adds write for group and others.
Nothing grants execute here.

options.t: It adds execute only to directories and to files that already have an execute bit for someone.
options.why: Convenient to open a tree for reading without making ordinary files executable.

options.t: It adds execute to every file.

It does the opposite for directories.

options.why: Often too much: ordinary files get an execute bit.
`-R` descends.

questions.title: Give the team write access
questions.text: You want your group to be able to edit `plan.txt`, which is currently `rw-r-----` and owned by you with another group. Put the steps in order.

items.t: Look at the current owner and group with `ls -l plan.txt`
items.why: Always check the current state first.

questions.title: What umask does
questions.text: What does the `umask` do?

options.t: It defines which permission bits are removed from newly created files and directories.
options.why: Applied by the creating process, before you ever see the new file.

options.t: It changes the permissions of all existing files.
options.why: It does not touch existing files.

options.t: It sets the owner of new files.
options.why: Ownership comes from the creating user.
That has nothing to do with permissions.

questions.title: Default file permissions
questions.text: With `umask 022`, a new directory gets mode `{{0}}` and a new regular file gets `{{1}}`.
questions.note: Directories start from 777, files from 666 (files never get execute automatically), then the umask bits are removed.

wrong.why: Directories start from 777; the umask removes 022 from it.
That is the starting point for files, before the umask is applied.

questions.title: Private files
questions.text: To make new files readable and writable only by you (and new directories accessible only to you) set `umask {{0}}`
questions.note: 077 removes every bit from group and others.

wrong.why: That would *remove* all permissions from the owner and give nothing to the rest, because the umask says what to take away.

pairs.why: Group can write too: common with private groups.

questions.text: After `umask 0174`, what mode does a new **directory** get?

options.why: 777 with the bits 1, 7 and 4 removed per class: 6, 0, 3.
The umask says what is removed, not what is set.

questions.title: Same umask, new file

questions.title: Numeric umask is not subtraction
questions.text: `umask 033` with a new file: 666 minus 033 gives 633 by subtraction. Why is the real result 644 (`rw-r--r--`)?

options.t: The umask clears bits, it does not subtract numbers: 033 clears `w` and `x` for group and others, so `rw-` (6) loses only its `w` and becomes `r--` (4); plain subtraction would give 6-3=3 (`-wx`), a nonsense mode.
options.why: Bitwise, not arithmetic. For files the result is 6, 4, 4, and subtracting would wrongly suggest 633.

options.t: Because subtraction is correct but the shell prints a different value.
options.why: The bit logic is the real rule.
It depends on the umask.

options.t: Because the umask applies only to directories.
options.why: It applies to files too.

options.t: It affects only that shell and the programs it starts from now on; other terminals keep their own umask.
options.why: To keep it, put the line in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.profile`.

options.t: It changes the umask of the whole system for every user.
options.why: It is a per-process setting inherited by children.

options.t: It is stored on disk and survives a reboot.
options.why: Not unless you put it in a startup file.

options.t: It changes the mode of existing files.
options.why: Only new files are affected.

questions.text: Match each description to the special bit.

questions.title: The /tmp directory
questions.text: Why is `/tmp` mode `drwxrwxrwt` and not just `drwxrwxrwx`?

options.t: The sticky bit (`t`) stops users from deleting or renaming files that belong to other users, although everyone can write there.
options.why: Without it, anyone could remove anyone else's temporary files.

options.t: The `t` means the directory is temporary and deleted at shutdown.
options.why: Clean-up of `/tmp` is done by other mechanisms.

options.t: It means the contents are encrypted.
options.why: Not related.

options.t: It means only the owner can list the directory.
options.why: Listing still needs `r`.

options.t: They are always readable by everyone, which leaks secrets.
options.why: Readability is not the concern.
